system: You synthesise research taste. Output only JSON.
prompt:
Below are verified evidence items from one AI-safety researcher's documents, all dated before 2026. Each item contrasts what a typical strong ML-safety researcher would do (default) with what his work did (his choice). Fields: id [date; decision point; distinct = 1-3, how strongly a typical researcher would take the default; own = his choice, team = co-authored middle-author work].

Task: synthesise at most 12 claims that capture what DISTINGUISHES this researcher from the field, the choices someone who knows only field consensus would predict wrongly.

Rules:
- Each claim must recur: supported by items from at least 2 different documents, or by one item with distinct = 3 and attribution own. Prefer own items.
- Drop anything that is field consensus (controls, hedging, replication, realism, rigour, caring about safety). A claim like "he is careful about confounds" is worthless here.
- Prefer claims that would change a prediction about a concrete research decision: which question to study, which paradigm, which models, what to do with a surprising result, what to publish and how.
- Claims must not name him, his co-authors, papers, datasets or specific results, so they generalise to new projects.
- For each claim write a gate item that a blind judge will see without knowing who the researcher is:
  - context: 1-2 neutral sentences describing a generic research decision where the claim applies. No names.
  - his_option: one sentence, the option he would take.
  - default_option: one sentence, the option a typical strong ML-safety researcher would take. Write it faithfully and in the same tone, length and level of specificity as his_option. Do not make either option sound sloppy, timid, reckless or obviously worse.
- evidence: 2-4 item ids, strongest first.

Return ONLY a JSON object:
{"claims": [{"id": "K1", "claim": "When <generic situation>, he <choice> rather than <default>.", "dpoint": "Q|D1|...|D6", "context": "...", "his_option": "...", "default_option": "...", "evidence": ["C12", "C40"]}]}

C2 [2025-12-17; D1; distinct=2; team] default: Train or tune the interpretability method on the target kind of model or task, or use a model-organism setup the method has seen. || his choice: Train the oracle only on the base model's activations and apply it zero-shot to fine-tuned variants, so the evaluation tests whether weights-only knowledge can be verbalized. || why: Knowledge in the fine-tuned models exists only in weights and never in the input text, so success requires substantial generalization.
C3 [2025-12-17; D2; distinct=2; team] default: Pour effort into curated, task-relevant supervised datasets, including SAE-feature interpretation, for the oracle. || his choice: Add a self-supervised context-prediction task (predict previous/next tokens from activations) on pretraining and chat text as a scalable, unlimited data source. || why: It enables unlimited training data from any text corpus and adds diversity of activation-verbalization signal.

C20 [2024-05-13; Q; distinct=2; own] default: Study explanation faithfulness via interpretability or by testing whether chain-of-thought explanations reflect biasing features (as in Turpin et al.). || his choice: Asks whether a model can introspectively articulate in natural language the rule that describes its own classification behaviour, a self-explanation capability, with behavioural ground truth. || why: Models may have the conceptual sophistication and capacity to use an internal process and reflect on it; black-box evaluation avoids needing to localize and interpret components.
